name: step-ca
description: Private certificate authority with a real ACME server, so internal clients renew certificates exactly the way they renew public ones.
value: step-ca Private certificate authority and ACME server Security Operations and Forensics

offline.why: This is the item that decides whether HTTPS survives a block. Public certificates are capped at 47 days by 2029 and every renewal is a round trip to a CA you do not control — one filtering event and your whole intranet expires on a timer. A 10-year internal root distributed once, with ACME behind it, makes the renewal loop entirely local. The cost is real: you must get the root into every browser, phone and Java trust store in the building, and that is a day of work you will repeat for every new device.

name: chrony (+ GPS/PPS)

offline.why: The most underrated item in the whole stack. Cut the WAN and clocks drift; drifted clocks break TLS validation, TOTP logins, DICOM timestamps and any attempt to correlate logs across machines — and they break them three weeks later, when nobody connects the two events. A GPS/PPS hat on a Raspberry Pi is about 90 USD and removes the entire failure class. chrony over ntpd because it converges fast after a cold boot, which is what you get after a power event.
offline.install: chrony.conf: refclock SHM 0 refid NMEA offset 0.5 + refclock PPS /dev/pps0 lock NMEA

alts.note: no satellites needed, drifts more, but it is 3 USD and better than nothing

name: OpenZFS
description: Copy-on-write filesystem with checksums, snapshots, native encryption, and send/receive replication.
value: OpenZFS Copy-on-write filesystem with checksums, snapshots, native encryption, and send/receive replication. storage filesystem raidz snapshots checksums encryption offline self-hosted

offline.why: Checksums are the point. Every other RAID will happily hand you a silently corrupted file and report success; ZFS tells you which file and, with RAIDZ2, fixes it. The costs are real and people discover them late: you cannot grow a RAIDZ vdev by one disk the way you grow mdadm (RAIDZ expansion landed in 2024 and is still slow and awkward), ECC memory genuinely matters, and a pool past 80% full gets noticeably slower.
offline.ram: 1 GB per TB is a rule of thumb, not a requirement
offline.install: zpool create -o ashift=12 tank raidz2 /dev/disk/by-id/...   then zfs create -o encryption=on tank/data

alts.note: in-kernel and flexible; RAID5/6 still not recommended for data you care about

name: restic
description: Deduplicating, encrypted, incremental backup to a local disk, an external HDD or an SFTP target.
value: restic Deduplicating, encrypted, incremental backup to a local disk, an external HDD or an SFTP target. storage backup encryption dedup verify offline self-hosted

offline.why: ZFS snapshots are not backups — they die with the pool. restic is the layer that leaves the machine, and it encrypts by default so a rotated cold drive that gets lost is an inconvenience rather than a disclosure. Its verification story is what earns it a slot: restic check --read-data actually reads every byte back, which is the only way to learn that a cold drive rotted before you need it.
offline.install: restic -r /mnt/cold/repo init && restic -r /mnt/cold/repo backup /srv

alts.note: faster on huge repos, but the repository format is not portable to object storage

name: par2cmdline
description: Generates Reed-Solomon recovery files so a damaged archive can be reconstructed from the surviving bytes.
value: par2cmdline Generates Reed-Solomon recovery files so a damaged archive can be reconstructed from the surviving bytes. storage sneakernet optical recovery integrity offline self-hosted

offline.why: Optical media is the layer that survives everything, and it is also the layer that develops unreadable sectors in a drawer. Ten percent PAR2 redundancy costs 10 GB on a 100 GB disc and converts most scratches and early rot from a total loss into a rebuild. Every disc that leaves the building gets SHA256SUMS and a .par2 set at the root, no exceptions — a checksum only tells you the disc is dead, PAR2 gets the data back.
offline.install: par2 create -r10 -n1 archive.par2 ./*   then par2 verify archive.par2

alts.note: same format, several times faster on modern CPUs
purpose-built for optical, but effectively unmaintained

name: LanCache
description: Transparent caching proxy for game and platform CDNs: one machine downloads a 120 GB game, every other machine on the LAN gets it at line speed.

offline.why: The highest value-per-effort container in the entire plan for anyone with more than one gaming machine. It works by DNS: you point clients at the lancache-dns container, which answers CDN hostnames with the cache's address. That also means it fits the split-horizon design exactly, and it turns a throttled or intermittent WAN into a non-issue for bulk downloads even when nothing is censored. Budget 2–5 TB and put it on spinning disks; it is sequential, large-file traffic.

name: Minecraft (Java server)
description: The official Java Edition server jar, which can be told to stop checking player identities against Mojang's session servers.
value: Minecraft (Java server) The official Java Edition server jar, which can be told to stop checking player identities against Mojang's session servers. games sandbox lan account offline-mode offline self-hosted

offline.why: Setting online-mode=false in server.properties makes the server join-able with no internet at all — the catch is that it also means the server trusts whatever username a client claims, so it belongs on a trusted VLAN and nowhere else. The harder half is the client: the official launcher only enters offline mode after a successful online login, so keep a launcher that supports offline profiles and keep the version jars cached locally before you need them.
offline.escape: online-mode=false on the server, plus a client launcher with genuine offline profile support and the asset/version files already downloaded. Do the caching now, not during the outage.
offline.install: java -Xmx4G -jar server.jar nogui   with online-mode=false in server.properties

name: Steam (Offline Mode)
description: Runs an already-installed library without a connection, provided it was signed in recently and the individual title has no additional DRM.
value: Steam (Offline Mode) Runs an already-installed library without a connection, provided it was signed in recently and the individual title has no additional DRM. games drm account warning best-effort offline self-hosted

offline.why: Best-effort, never a foundation. Offline Mode needs a successful online login on that machine reasonably recently, breaks if the client decides it must update, and covers only titles whose own DRM cooperates — anything with a third-party launcher or a companion account on top will refuse regardless. Combine it with LanCache to make the pre-download painless, then assume nothing about it during a long outage.
offline.escape: Log in and enter Offline Mode deliberately before the outage, pre-download everything you want, and disable client auto-updates. Where a title exists on GOG, buy it there instead.

name: GOG offline installers
description: Sells games as standalone installer files with no DRM, no launcher requirement and no activation.
value: GOG offline installers Sells games as standalone installer files with no DRM, no launcher requirement and no activation. games drm-free purchase archive installers offline self-hosted

offline.why: The single most offline-friendly source of commercial games that exists, and it should be the default place to buy. The important habit is not buying there — it is downloading the offline installers immediately and archiving them alongside their checksums, because purchase history lives on their servers and your archive lives on your shelf. A game you own but have not downloaded is a game you do not have.
offline.escape: Fetch every purchased installer while online and store the files with SHA256SUMS. After that they need nothing, forever.
offline.install: Download the offline backup installers from the account library, verify, then archive to disc

alts.note: also DRM-free by default, much smaller catalogue

name: aptly
description: Mirrors, snapshots and publishes Debian and Ubuntu repositories, including your own signed packages.
value: aptly Mirrors, snapshots and publishes Debian and Ubuntu repositories, including your own signed packages. mirrors debian ubuntu apt snapshots offline self-hosted

offline.why: The snapshot model is what distinguishes it from apt-mirror: you can pin a known-good state of the archive, test against it, publish it, and roll back if an update breaks a machine — which matters far more when the fix cannot simply be re-downloaded. Mirror only the suites and architectures you actually run; a full Ubuntu LTS mirror for amd64 and arm64 is on the order of 800 GB, and most of it is packages nobody in the building will ever install.
offline.escape: Refresh monthly while the WAN is up. An unmirrored security update is not a resilience problem until it is.
offline.disk: ~800 GB for a selective Debian/Ubuntu mirror
offline.install: aptly mirror create -architectures=amd64 noble http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main && aptly mirror update noble

alts.note: much simpler, no snapshots, no publishing

name: dnf reposync + createrepo_c
description: Pulls a Fedora, RHEL or Rocky repository to local disk and regenerates the metadata so clients can install from it.
value: dnf reposync + createrepo_c Pulls a Fedora, RHEL or Rocky repository to local disk and regenerates the metadata so clients can install from it. mirrors fedora rpm rsync repository offline self-hosted

offline.why: No extra software to run and nothing to keep alive — the mirror is a directory served by the web server you already have. Mirror the current release and n-1 only, for the one architecture you deploy; that is roughly 600 GB, versus several terabytes if you take everything. Remember --download-metadata, or you will have every package and no way for dnf to find them.
offline.escape: Re-run monthly. Keep the previous tree until the new one has been installed from successfully at least once.
offline.disk: ~600 GB for current + n-1, one architecture
offline.install: dnf reposync --repoid=fedora --download-metadata -p /srv/mirror

name: devpi
description: Caching PyPI proxy that stores every package it has ever served and keeps serving it when upstream is unreachable.
value: devpi Caching PyPI proxy that stores every package it has ever served and keeps serving it when upstream is unreachable. mirrors pypi python pull-through cache offline self-hosted

offline.why: Pull-through beats mirroring for Python: full PyPI is enormous and almost entirely irrelevant to you, whereas devpi ends up holding exactly the dependency closure your projects actually build against. Point pip at it from day one, well before you need it — a cache is only worth what passed through it, and one started during the outage is empty.
offline.escape: Set index-url in pip.conf on every machine now, and run a build of each project you care about while online so the closure is warm.
offline.disk: grows with use; ~200 GB is generous
offline.install: pip install devpi-server && devpi-init && devpi-server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3141

name: Verdaccio
description: Lightweight npm registry that proxies the public registry, caches every tarball it serves, and hosts private packages.
value: Verdaccio Lightweight npm registry that proxies the public registry, caches every tarball it serves, and hosts private packages. mirrors npm javascript pull-through cache offline self-hosted

offline.why: The npm equivalent of devpi and the same argument applies, with more urgency: a JavaScript project's dependency tree is thousands of tarballs and any one of them missing fails the whole install. It also solves a problem that has nothing to do with censorship — a package unpublished or yanked upstream stays in your cache.
offline.escape: Configure .npmrc registry on every workstation now and install each project once while online to warm the cache.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 4873:4873 -v /verdaccio:/verdaccio/storage verdaccio/verdaccio

name: Distribution (registry:2)
description: The reference container registry, which in pull-through mode transparently caches every image pulled through it.
value: Distribution (registry:2) The reference container registry, which in pull-through mode transparently caches every image pulled through it. mirrors containers docker pull-through images offline self-hosted

offline.why: Without this, a rebooted Docker host with no WAN cannot start anything it has not already pulled, and that is the most common way a self-hosted stack dies during an outage. Two caveats worth knowing before you rely on it: a pull-through cache mirrors one upstream registry, so ghcr.io and quay.io need their own instances, and the cache does not protect you from a tag being retagged — pin digests for anything critical.
offline.escape: Configure registry-mirrors in daemon.json on every host, and pull the images of every service you run at least once. Better still, docker save the critical few to a tarball on the archive disc.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 -e REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io registry:2

alts.note: adds replication, RBAC and vulnerability scanning; also adds Postgres, Redis and real operational weight

name: Matrix Synapse
description: Reference Matrix homeserver: rooms, history, end-to-end encryption, file transfer, with Element as the client.
value: Matrix Synapse Reference Matrix homeserver: rooms, history, end-to-end encryption, file transfer, with Element as the client. comms chat matrix e2ee federation offline self-hosted

offline.why: Federation is what makes Matrix interesting and it is also the part that dies with the WAN — which is fine, because a homeserver whose users are all local does not need to federate at all. Run it closed and it is a complete chat system for the building. Be realistic about cost: Python, Postgres, and enough RAM that it is a poor fit for a Raspberry Pi. If chat is all you need, Prosody does it in a tenth of the resources.
offline.install: ghcr.io/element-hq/synapse with a Postgres sidecar; disable federation in homeserver.yaml

alts.note: XMPP, Lua, ~50 MB of RAM; less pretty, dramatically lighter
Rust homeserver, far smaller footprint, fewer features

name: Mumble
description: Low-latency voice chat server with positional audio and clients on every desktop platform.
value: Mumble Low-latency voice chat server with positional audio and clients on every desktop platform. comms voice low-latency lan lightweight offline self-hosted

offline.why: Old, small, and it simply works — a server process measured in megabytes that will carry a dozen people on a Raspberry Pi over the LAN with latency nobody notices. The certificate model is self-signed by design, which fits an internal CA neatly. It is voice only; if you need faces, that is Jitsi and a much larger conversation about WebRTC.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 64738:64738/tcp -p 64738:64738/udp mumblevoip/mumble-server

name: docker-mailserver
description: Postfix, Dovecot, SpamAssassin and the rest assembled into one container, configured through a handful of files.
value: docker-mailserver Postfix, Dovecot, SpamAssassin and the rest assembled into one container, configured through a handful of files. comms email smtp imap internal offline self-hosted

offline.why: Internal-only mail is a far easier problem than public mail — no reputation, no SPF politics, no fighting to stay out of a spam folder — and it gives you a working address for every device, cron job and appliance that only knows how to complain by email. Do not talk yourself into also making it your public mail server; that is a different, much less pleasant hobby.
offline.install: ghcr.io/docker-mailserver/docker-mailserver with a mailserver.env and setup.sh for accounts

name: PairDrop
description: Browser-to-browser file transfer between devices on the same network, with nothing to install on either end.
value: PairDrop Browser-to-browser file transfer between devices on the same network, with nothing to install on either end. comms file-transfer webrtc lan guests offline self-hosted

offline.why: The answer to a guest who needs to hand you a file and has an iPhone. Self-hosted, it discovers peers on the local network and moves the bytes directly over WebRTC — but a strict LAN needs its own STUN configuration or the connection negotiation quietly falls back to nothing. Test it with the WAN unplugged before you rely on it, which is advice that applies to this entire list.
offline.install: lscr.io/linuxserver/pairdrop, served over HTTPS (WebRTC will not run on plain HTTP)

name: Uptime Kuma
description: Status checks over HTTP, TCP, ICMP and DNS with a status page and notifications to almost anything.
value: Uptime Kuma Status checks over HTTP, TCP, ICMP and DNS with a status page and notifications to almost anything. ops monitoring status alerts certificates offline self-hosted

offline.why: Ten minutes to install and it will tell you a certificate is expiring or a container did not come back after a reboot. Two adjustments for an offline box: point the notification channel at your own Matrix or SMTP rather than a push service that needs the WAN, and add explicit monitors for the boring infrastructure — DNS answering, the CA responding, NTP stratum — because those are the ones whose failure you notice last.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 3001:3001 -v uptime-kuma:/app/data louislam/uptime-kuma

name: Prometheus + Grafana
description: Scrapes metrics from node_exporter and friends, stores the time series locally, and draws them.
value: Prometheus + Grafana Scrapes metrics from node_exporter and friends, stores the time series locally, and draws them. ops metrics dashboards trends smart offline self-hosted

offline.why: Uptime Kuma tells you something is down; this tells you a disk has been getting slower for three weeks. That distinction is what justifies the extra complexity, and only that — if you will not look at the dashboards, run neither. One offline trap: Grafana's dashboard import and plugin catalogue both fetch from grafana.com, so provision dashboards from JSON files on disk and install plugins before you need them.
offline.disk: retention-dependent; 50 GB is plenty at home scale
offline.install: prom/prometheus + grafana/grafana, with prometheus/node-exporter on each host

name: Homepage
description: Configurable dashboard of links and live service widgets, defined entirely in YAML files.
value: Homepage Configurable dashboard of links and live service widgets, defined entirely in YAML files. ops dashboard landing-page yaml kiosk offline self-hosted

offline.why: The landing page is what makes an intranet feel like a product instead of a list of ports, and it is the page a printed QR code should point at. One thing to fix on day one: it resolves service icons from a remote icon CDN by default, which is a WAN dependency on your offline home page. Drop the icon set into the local icons directory and reference it with sh- or the local path instead.
offline.install: ghcr.io/gethomepage/homepage with config/ mounted; set HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS

alts.note: no widgets, no updates, never breaks — genuinely worth considering

name: Network UPS Tools
description: Reads the UPS over USB or serial and shuts hosts down cleanly in a defined order when the battery runs low.
value: Network UPS Tools Reads the UPS over USB or serial and shuts hosts down cleanly in a defined order when the battery runs low. ops ups power shutdown lifepo4 offline self-hosted

offline.why: A UPS without NUT is a device that delays the unclean shutdown by nine minutes. The part people get wrong is ordering: the storage node must be the last thing to power off and the first to come back, and the hypervisor must stop its guests before the pool goes away. Write that order down, put it in the printed runbook, and test it by actually pulling the mains — power events are the most likely outage on this whole list, well ahead of censorship.
offline.install: ups.conf: driver = usbhid-ups, port = auto   then enable nut-server and nut-monitor

name: Forgejo
description: Self-hosted Git forge with issues, releases, LFS and a container registry, in a single Go binary.
value: Forgejo Self-hosted Git forge with issues, releases, LFS and a container registry, in a single Go binary. ops git forge lfs mirror bundles offline self-hosted

offline.why: Two jobs here. It is where every fleet repository lives locally so a seized account or a blocked host costs nothing, and it is the mirror for the 3D-print model library — every model you actually print, committed with its licence file, its sliced gcode and its printer profile. A model you cannot print during an outage is not a model you have. Pair it with git bundle for the crown-jewel discs: one self-contained, clonable file per repository.
offline.install: codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:latest with a data volume; SQLite is fine below ~20 users

alts.note: the codebase Forgejo forked from; corporate governance is the only real difference

name: Vaultwarden
description: Compatible reimplementation of the Bitwarden server in Rust, serving the official Bitwarden clients.
value: Vaultwarden Compatible reimplementation of the Bitwarden server in Rust, serving the official Bitwarden clients. security passwords totp bitwarden vault offline self-hosted

offline.why: Passwords and TOTP seeds on your own hardware, with clients that already exist for every platform and cache the vault locally so a phone still opens it with the server unreachable. The failure mode to plan for is not a breach, it is a lockout: an encrypted export in the fire safe and the important credentials on paper, because a self-hosted vault whose host is down and whose owner forgot the master password is unrecoverable by design.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 8080:80 -v /vw-data:/data vaultwarden/server

name: CrowdSec
description: Parses logs for attack patterns and pushes decisions to a bouncer in the firewall or reverse proxy.
value: CrowdSec Parses logs for attack patterns and pushes decisions to a bouncer in the firewall or reverse proxy. security ips logs firewall wan-facing offline self-hosted

offline.why: Relevant only to whatever you still expose to the WAN, which in this architecture should be very little. Its selling point is a shared reputation feed, and that feed is exactly the part that stops working offline — the local detection engine keeps banning what it sees, it just no longer knows what the rest of the world is seeing. Judge it on the local half, because that is the half you keep.
offline.escape: Install collections and parsers while online. The engine and its bouncers then run entirely locally; only the community blocklist goes stale.
offline.install: cscli collections install crowdsecurity/nginx && cscli bouncers add caddy

alts.note: no cloud component whatsoever; that is both the argument for and against it

name: age
description: File encryption with small public keys, one obvious command line and no configuration or key ring to maintain.
value: age File encryption with small public keys, one obvious command line and no configuration or key ring to maintain. security encryption archive m-disc keys offline self-hosted

offline.why: The right tool for the archive layer: encrypting a tarball before it goes to an M-DISC or a cold drive should be one command that will still be one command in ten years. GnuPG can do this and also four hundred other things, and its complexity is how people end up with an archive they cannot open. Whatever you choose, the recipient key belongs on paper in the safe — an offline plan that loses its keys is worse than no plan.
offline.install: age-keygen -o key.txt   then age -R recipients.txt -o archive.tar.age archive.tar

alts.note: universal and expected by others; far more ways to get it wrong

name: whisper.cpp
description: Speech-to-text transcription from a single C++ binary and one model file, on CPU or GPU.
value: whisper.cpp Speech-to-text transcription from a single C++ binary and one model file, on CPU or GPU. ai transcription speech cpu spanish offline self-hosted

offline.why: Transcription is the highest-value offline AI task after search, because it converts the one media type you cannot grep — recorded speech — into something Paperless can index. large-v3 is about 3 GB and runs at better than real time on a modern CPU, so the GPU is optional here. Spanish accuracy is good; heavily accented or overlapping speech still needs a human pass.
offline.install: whisper-cli -m models/ggml-large-v3.bin -l es -f audio.wav

name: LibreTranslate
description: Self-hosted translation API over Argos Translate models, with an HTTP endpoint and a small web UI.
value: LibreTranslate Self-hosted translation API over Argos Translate models, with an HTTP endpoint and a small web UI. ai translation api argos languages offline self-hosted

offline.why: Machine translation is the least obvious dependency in the pile: it is embedded in browsers, phones and half the tools people use daily, and every one of those routes text to a vendor. Load only the language pairs you use — --load-only es,en keeps the memory footprint sane — and accept that quality sits below the large commercial engines. For understanding a datasheet or drafting an email, that gap does not matter.
offline.install: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 libretranslate/libretranslate --load-only es,en

name: ComfyUI
description: Node-graph interface for local image diffusion models, with every step of the pipeline exposed.
value: ComfyUI Node-graph interface for local image diffusion models, with every step of the pipeline exposed. ai diffusion images gpu print offline self-hosted

offline.why: The honest ranking puts this last among the AI items: it is the one that produces the most visible output and solves the fewest actual problems during an outage. It earns a place for illustration and print work — disc art, labels, signage — that would otherwise mean a subscription and an upload. Its extension ecosystem installs code from arbitrary repositories, which is a real supply-chain surface on a machine you are hardening; pin what you install and stop there.
offline.ram: 8 GB VRAM for comfortable SDXL-class work
offline.install: git clone, pip install -r requirements.txt, python main.py --listen

name: dcm4chee-arc-light
description: Full enterprise DICOM archive: IOCM, HL7 integration, modality worklist, retention policies and audit logging.
value: dcm4chee-arc-light Full enterprise DICOM archive: IOCM, HL7 integration, modality worklist, retention policies and audit logging. medical dicom archive hl7 audit enterprise offline self-hosted

offline.why: What you deploy when Orthanc is genuinely outgrown, and not before. It is a Java EE application with PostgreSQL and an LDAP configuration store behind it, which means real capability and real operational cost — the configuration lives in LDAP, so backing it up is not the same task as backing up the images. The audit trail is the reason a hospital picks it and the reason it survives an inspection.
offline.install: docker compose with dcm4che/dcm4chee-arc-psql, a PostgreSQL and an LDAP container

name: OHIF Viewer
description: Browser-based DICOM viewer that reads studies from any DICOMweb endpoint, served as static files.
value: OHIF Viewer Browser-based DICOM viewer that reads studies from any DICOMweb endpoint, served as static files. medical viewer dicomweb browser static offline self-hosted

offline.why: Static HTML and JavaScript over DICOMweb means it deploys the same way the rest of this fleet does — copy the build directory behind the reverse proxy, point it at Orthanc, done. That makes it the right viewer for a referring physician or a kiosk, where installing a desktop application is not going to happen. For primary diagnosis, use a calibrated workstation and a validated viewer; a browser on an uncalibrated monitor is not that.
offline.install: Serve the built static bundle and set the DICOMweb data source to your Orthanc
